transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-10 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Location: Zoom / Recorded
Shared artifacts: deck: https://redwood.in/briefs/noisy-neighbor, perf sheet: https://redwood.in/sheets/kv-batching-Cobalt13B (note: placeholders)

Attendees: Kayla (Redwood AE), Miguel (SE), Priya (SA), Jared (Cobalt), Aria (Cobalt), Samir (Cobalt), Maya (Cobalt security)

Summary (auto): Deep dive on isolation and mitigation strategies for noisy neighbor, tail-latency reduction via KV cache and continuous batching, quantization tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Hosted, VPC/on-prem networking constraints, and the pilot plan.

[00:00:00] Kayla: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros? we have about 75 minutes, want to cover isolation strategies, then go into batching and kv cache numbers, and finish with pilot next steps.
[00:00:12] Jared: thanks Kayla. Jared here - platform eng. Aria, Samir, Maya on the line. we run a multi-tenant inference layer today on k8s. main pain is noisy neighbor — spikes from our ingest pipeline kill tail p99.
[00:00:25] Miguel: picked up. are those spikes from long-context chat sessions or from batch scoring jobs?
[00:00:28] Aria: mostly chat sessions — variable seq lengths, plus occasional batch reranks that run during off-peak but sometimes overlap. we see token-level throttling but p99 gets bad.
[00:00:38] Priya: can you share current sla targets? what p99 are you shooting for?
[00:00:41] Samir: our product target is 300ms p95 for 8k-context 13B but p99 we tolerate up to 1.5s. however certain enterprise customers expect tighter.
[00:00:51] Miguel: ok, good. quick orientation: on Redwood Dedicated we offer capacity fencing — you get a GPU pool pinned to your tenancy, plus runtime guardrails that limit other tenants. Hosted has multi-tenant fast path with nicer cost but potential noisy neighbor unless you opt for dedicated pools.
[00:01:06] Maya: question — for on-prem/private deployment, how does KV cache persist across restarts? we need to maintain cache for session continuity and also for audit reasons.
[00:01:14] Priya: good question. in private we ship optional KV cache persistence to an S3-compatible store with encryption-in-transit and at-rest keys via KMS. metadata is logged to audit trail. note: we can enable stricter retention controls for healthcare regs.
[00:01:29] Aria: sweet. can you talk about tail-latency mitigations aside from capacity fencing? like preemption, throttling, or priority queues?
[00:01:36] Miguel: sure — several layers. 1) routing by priority: low-latency traffic goes to pinned instances; 2) continuous batching with windowing tuned to preserve p99; 3) prefix/KV caching which reduces decoding tokens; 4) graceful fallback to cheaper model variants when latency SLO is jeopardized. also admission control to shed large batch jobs when the pool reaches saturation.
[00:01:56] [00:02:00] Kayla: can you expand continuous batching — customers often worry batching increases tail latency.
[00:02:05] Miguel: Absolutely — our runtime implements adaptive windowing: if arrival rate is high, batch size grows to improve throughput but with a hard cap on wait time (e.g., 8ms) to bound added latency. we also do sequence-length aware packing — shorter requests are co-packed with long ones to reduce wasted compute. experimental results show p95 improves significantly while p99 is kept within SLO with proper config.
[00:02:29] Aria: hmm, sequences are quite bimodal for us — quick single-turn queries and long sessions — how does packing avoid head-of-line blocking?
[00:02:37] Miguel: we use multi-queue packing: separate queues by estimated token length. small requests can be placed in a low-latency queue with smaller max-window. we also have a preemptive slot system so a tiny request can jump into an earlier execution slot if a large request is still accumulating. but this increases scheduling complexity.
[00:02:56] Jared: are these configs exposed to us? we need to tune per-team.
[00:02:59] Priya: yes, through Redwood Console you can set per-route policies: max wait, priority label, model variant fallback, and caching TTL. for Dedicated we can also apply node-level QoS to isolate shards.
[00:03:12] [00:03:15] Aria: on KV cache — curious about eviction policies and cold-start penalty. we saw big p99 spikes when the KV cache misses for long-session chat.
[00:03:22] Miguel: typical eviction is LRU with size-tiering by prefix frequency. but for long-session workloads you can pin prefixes to a session-store, which keeps KV entries for a session's lifetime — useful if you have sticky sessions. cold-start penalty depends on model size and token depth; in our lab 13B single-GPU, a full KV warmup took ~300-700ms for worst-case sequences; with prefix caching we can shave that to ~60-120ms. caveat: numbers vary with quantization and kernel selection.
[00:03:48] Samir: quantization — are you recommending int8 or int4 for our use? we are worried about quality drift for clinical phrasing.
[00:03:55] Miguel: tradeoffs. int8 tends to be safe for 13B workloads with negligible quality delta on most evals; int4 is higher risk but gives 1.5-2x throughput gains and reduced memory so more isolation headroom per GPU. we suggest controlled evals on your LLM QA prompts. Redwood Optimize can run a regression check across your prompt suite.
[00:04:16] Maya: security-wise, if we do on-prem with KMS and HSM, any leakage risk from cache persist or from multi-tenant host?
[00:04:23] Priya: for Dedicated and private we ensure tenant isolation — kv cache is tenant-scoped. for hosted multi-tenant we encrypt cache entries and segregate keys. HSM-backed KMS integration is available for on-prem, and we produce audit logs for any access. we can provide SOC2 artifacts.
[00:04:38] [00:04:41] Jared: back to noisy neighbor mitigation — what about noisy-gpu jobs like large-batch offline scoring causing device memory pressure and evicting other processes?
[00:04:48] Miguel: two strategies: 1) capacity fencing (pin GPUs) so offline scoring runs on separate reserved nodes; 2) runtime-level preemption where large batch job can run with soft affinity and be throttled if it crosses memory thresholds; 3) memory-aware packing and kernel selection — smaller kernels for shorter contexts. for Dedicated we can guarantee node-level isolation to avoid eviction entirely.
[00:05:11] Aria: you mentioned fallback to cheaper model variants — for clinical outputs that raises QA concerns. how do you handle automatic fallback auditing?
[00:05:19] Priya: fallbacks are explicit and auditable in the routing policy. you can mark routes as "no-fallback" for sensitive customers. if fallback is allowed, the Console logs the reason (capacity, latency) and the model used; we also run sampling and QA checks to ensure quality doesn't regress.
[00:05:36] [00:05:40] Samir: ok can we see a real perf example? Miguel, run through the lab numbers you referenced earlier for 13B and mixed workload (40% short, 60% long).
[00:05:47] Miguel: sure — slide refs in the deck. lab config: 4x A10G GPU pool; model 13B quantized int8 baseline; arrival rate 120 rps aggregate. Results: hosted multi-tenant with batching window 12ms had throughput good but p99 ~1.1s on mixed workload; Dedicated pinned 4-GPU pool with priority routing and KV pinned sessions got p99 down to ~360ms, p95 ~220ms. enabling pinned prefixes reduced token decode counts average by 28%. switching to int4 improved throughput 1.8x but increased hallucination risk on certain clinical prompts by ~2.4% on our eval set.
[00:06:29] Aria: that delta on hallucination is concerning — can we limit int4 to non-critical routes?
[00:06:32] Miguel: absolutely — per-route quantization profiles are supported. you can have a high-fidelity route (fp16/int8) for clinical and an ops route (int4) for low-risk analytics.
[00:06:42] [00:06:45] Jared: how does VPC networking influence tail latency? our infra sits in a private VPC peered to cloud; we see sporadic network hiccups cause token spikes.
[00:06:53] Priya: VPC peering and egress paths matter. for Hosted traffic to cross cloud boundaries we recommend private link or VPC endpoints to reduce jitter. For private deployments inside your VPC, the network latency is usually consistent but you need to watch MTU, path MTU, and NAT gateway CPU; these can cause sporadic stalls for model shard fetches and cache pulls. We also support colocating the cache store (S3-compatible) inside the same VPC subnet to reduce network hops.
[00:07:17] Maya: regarding audit, do you keep logs of fallbacks and cache evictions? we need full traceability for compliance.
[00:07:22] Priya: yes — action logs include cache hits/misses, eviction events, model fallback events, routing decisions, and token-level timing traces. retention is configurable.
[00:07:31] [00:07:35] Miguel: wanted to surface an interesting mitigation — speculative decoding for tail-latency. we can speculatively decode top-K tokens in a faster, lower-precision path to get a quick preliminary output while continuing the high-fidelity pass. it helps for streaming use-cases where early tokens matter.
[00:07:51] Aria: interesting. does speculative decoding affect cost?
[00:07:54] Miguel: yes slightly, you run two passes for some tokens; but you can restrict speculation to the first N tokens or to routes where p99 sensitivity is high. it's a tunable knob.
[00:08:04] [00:08:10] Jared: any concrete SLA language for Dedicated? our procurement team asks for quantifiable SLOs for p95/p99 and noisy neighbor protections.
[00:08:16] Kayla: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets at the cluster level; we can include carve-outs for extreme load and DDoS. we typically commit to latency windows in the contract after an initial pilot and benchmarking phase. the legal team does require exact workload profile to instrument SLOs.
[00:08:33] Samir: pilot plan?
[00:08:36] Kayla: propose a 4-week pilot: week 0-1 baseline data and config, week 2 run KV-cache and batching experiments, week 3 isolated Dedicated run, week 4 handoff and SLO definition. deliverables: perf sheet, config recipes, audit package.
[00:08:50] Aria: we need that perf sheet to include our real prompts — we'll share 500 sample turns.
[00:08:55] Kayla: perfect — Aria, Jared, drop them to the shared folder.
[00:08:58] [00:09:05] (interruption, background noise)
[00:09:10] Miguel: quick thought on scheduling — if you expect daily large reranks at 02:00 local, schedule them into dedicated windows or a separate pool. mixing them risks noisy neighbor.
[00:09:20] Jared: we do night batches but sometimes reprocessing spills into the day. ops has been lax.
[00:09:24] Priya: ops policies can be enforced via route labels and resource quotas; we can also set burst gating so background jobs are throttled when latency-critical queues exceed thresholds.
[00:09:36] [00:10:00] Kayla: let's open the floor for questions from security and procurement. Maya?
[00:10:05] Maya: ok small details — for on-prem installer, does Redwood require root access? how do we lock images?
[00:10:11] Priya: we provide a containerized distribution; installer requires cluster-admin for initial bootstrap but afterwards you can lock RBAC. image signing is supported and we integrate with your container registry and admission controllers.
[00:10:24] Maya: good. also need a data flow diagram for audit.
[00:10:27] Kayla: we'll attach one to the follow-up.
[00:10:30] [00:10:40] Aria: anything about autoscaling and its effect on p99 — we saw spin-up cold starts cause p99 spikes.
[00:10:46] Miguel: for Dedicated we recommend warm pools and fast scale mechanisms. cold starts from model load are heavy; solution: keep hot model instances pinned for traffic or prefetch the KV before traffic spike windows. autoscaler delta should be tuned with pre-warmed containers.
[00:10:59] Jared: can you pre-warm with quantized parameters only? we want to avoid full-precision loads in the middle of day.
[00:11:06] Miguel: yes — you can pre-warm with intended quantization artifact, kernel set, and even cached KV prefixes for key customers.
[00:11:13] [00:11:20] Kayla: ok time check — 12 minutes in, plenty more to cover. let's go deeper on a failure mode: concurrent long-seq requests that push KV memory beyond capacity and cause eviction storms.
[00:11:31] Miguel: eviction storms happen when many new prefixes compete. strategies: 1) session-level pinning for high-value sessions; 2) write-through backpressure — when cache pressure high, admission control reduces new long sessions and routes them to fallback smaller context mode; 3) dynamic cache resizing informed by telemetry: increase cache footprint for a short window if pattern persists.
[00:11:55] Aria: dynamic resizing sounds risky for cost.
[00:11:58] Miguel: yes cost vs p99. we recommend policy-based resizing with cost caps and automated rollback. Redwood Optimize can alert when cost creeps above threshold.
[00:12:10] [00:12:20] Samir: about telemetry — can we get token-level traces per request to correlate where spikes originate?
[00:12:26] Priya: yes — we have token timing traces, per-token kernel time, queuing time, and network fetch times. we can ingest into your telemetry stack or provide via the Console.
[00:12:36] Maya: do you support SAML SSO for Console and RBAC per team?
[00:12:40] Kayla: yes SAML + SCIM provisioning, role-based access in Console.
[00:12:44] [00:12:50] (brief crosstalk)
[00:12:55] Miguel: one more interesting point — kernel selection heuristics can reduce tail variance. we pick kernels based on sequence length distribution at runtime; sometimes slower kernel with better memory locality yields better p99. it's non-intuitive but we've seen it.
[00:13:13] Aria: do you expose kernel choices?
[00:13:15] Miguel: exposed as profiles in the Dedicated config; on hosted we auto-select but we can surface telemetry for tuning.
[00:13:23] [00:13:30] Jared: procurement will want contract language about noisy neighbor mitigation — e.g., dedicated pool guarantee. are there remediation credits?
[00:13:36] Kayla: yes we can include remediation and service credits for breaches of agreed SLOs on Dedicated. specifics in legal.
[00:13:42] Samir: final question — what happens if a node-level hardware failure happens mid-session? do you have transparent failover?
[00:13:48] Miguel: runtime has KV checkpointing and session handoff. for Dedicated we do cross-node redundancy for active sessions optionally; fallback is to restart session on another node and replay from last KV checkpoint. there is recovery latency but session continuity is possible.
[00:14:03] [00:14:10] Kayla: ok let's recap and next steps. Miguel, summarize the hard recommendations?
[00:14:15] Miguel: sure — 1) for Cobalt: start Dedicated pilot with 4-GPU fenced pool; 2) enable session pinning for high-value clinical customers; 3) use int8 for clinical routes and int4 only on analytics routes behind QA; 4) tune batching: multi-queue packing with 8ms hard cap for low-latency; 5) persist KV in VPC-local S3 with KMS; 6) configure pre-warm and warm pool autoscaling; 7) enable token traces for root-cause troubleshooting.
[00:14:44] Kayla: great. Jared/Aria, you'll share real prompts and p99 targets. we'll run the bench and shoot for the week of 12/29 to review.
[00:14:54] Aria: yes will upload 500 prompts by EOD tomorrow.
[00:14:57] Jared: procurement will expect SOC2 docs and the remediation clause.
[00:15:00] Kayla: sending SOC2 and on-prem package by 12/17.
[00:15:04] Maya: thanks, please add dataflow diagram.
[00:15:07] Kayla: will do.
[00:15:10] (wrap up pleasantries)
